qs.q: If a large pleural effusion is present, how might it affect the mediastinum?
o: Cause superior displacement of the aortic arch
Pull the mediastinum toward the affected side
Keep the mediastinum strictly central without movement
Push the mediastinum away from the affected side
qs.e: A large effusion exerts mass effect and pushes the mediastinum away from the affected side. Collapse pulls structures toward the abnormal side.

qs.q: A 63-year-old woman has sudden 'knife-like' chest pain radiating to the back, poorly controlled hypertension, and a widened mediastinum on CXR. CK is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Sudden, severe, tearing chest pain radiating to the back, a history of hypertension, and a widened mediastinum on CXR are classic signs of aortic dissection. Normal CK rules out acute MI.

qs.q: A 42-year-old male presents after a binge drinking episode with haematemesis. Endoscopy shows linear tears crossing the gastroesophageal junction without perforation into the mediastinum. What distinguishes this from Boerhaave syndrome?
o: Mallory-Weiss requires surgical repair while Boerhaave heals spontaneously
Mallory-Weiss tears occur in the stomach while Boerhaave occurs in the oesophagus
Mallory-Weiss tears are caused by alcohol while Boerhaave is caused by vomiting
Mallory-Weiss tears are superficial while Boerhaave involves transmural perforation
qs.e: Mallory-Weiss tears are superficial mucosal lacerations that heal spontaneously. Boerhaave syndrome involves transmural perforation leading to mediastinitis — a life-threatening surgical emergency.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thorax between the lungs, containing heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus and lymphatics. Its divisions guide diagnosis of masses, effusions and trauma.

sections.p: The mediastinum separates the right and left pleural cavities and houses vital structures. Clinicians use its borders to locate disease on imaging and to plan interventions.
b: Divided into superior and inferior parts; inferior further into anterior, middle, posterior

sections.p: Superior mediastinum extends from the thoracic inlet to the sternal angle; inferior lies below to the diaphragm. Anterior contains thymus, fat; middle holds heart, pericardium, roots of great vessels; posterior contains esophagus, thoracic aorta, thoracic duct.
b: Boundaries are easy landmarks on chest X‑ray and CT

sections.p: Anteriorly the sternum and costal cartilages; posteriorly the vertebral bodies and thoracic spine; laterally the pleural cavities; superiorly the thoracic inlet; inferiorly the diaphragm and upper abdomen.
b: Mediastinal shift on tension pneumothorax or large effusion indicates pressure effect

sections.p: Arterial supply comes from branches of the internal thoracic, bronchial, and intercostal arteries; venous drainage follows the azygos system and internal thoracic veins.
b: Bleeding from these vessels can cause rapid mediastinal hematoma

sections.p: Autonomic fibers from the vagus and sympathetic trunks run through the posterior mediastinum, providing parasympathetic innervation to heart and lungs.
b: Vagal injury may cause bradyarrhythmias after thoracic surgery

sections.p: Provides a protected conduit for the heart, great vessels, airway, esophagus and lymphatics, allowing coordinated cardiopulmonary function and immune surveillance.
b: Space constraints mean any mass quickly affects neighboring structures

sections.p: Mediastinal widening on X‑ray suggests mass, hemorrhage, or large effusion. Tension pneumothorax pushes mediastinum away, flattening the diaphragm. Effusions are classified by protein: exudate (>3 g/dL) often TB; transudate (low protein) often heart failure.
b: Stony dull percussion, absent breath sounds, reduced fremitus → pleural effusion
Bronchial breathing at upper edge → fluid level
Mediastinal shift → tension pneumothorax or large mass

t.b: Does the mediastinum appear widened or shifted? → Suggests mass, large effusion, or tension pneumothorax
Is protein >3 g/dL? → Exudate (TB, empyema); low protein → transudate (CHF, hypoalbuminemia)
What is the exact compartment of a mediastinal mass? → Guides biopsy and management

sections.p: Remember the four mediastinal compartments and the classic causes of anterior (thymoma, lymphoma, germ cell tumor, thyroid), middle (lymphadenopathy, cysts, vascular), and posterior (neurogenic tumors, esophageal) masses.
b: Anterior: “4 T’s” – Thymoma, Teratoma, Thyroid, Terrible lymphoma
Middle: bronchogenic cyst, lymph node enlargement (TB, HIV)
Posterior: schwannoma, neurofibroma, esophageal duplication cyst

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden mediastinal shift with respiratory distress (tension pneumothorax)
Large pleural effusion causing hemodynamic compromise
Rapidly enlarging mediastinal mass with superior vena cava syndrome

faq.q: Why does a large pleural effusion push the mediastinum away?
faq.a: The fluid creates pressure that displaces the flexible mediastinal structures toward the opposite side.

faq.q: How can you tell an exudative from a transudative effusion without a lab?
faq.a: Clinically, exudates often accompany fever, weight loss, or TB risk; transudates occur with heart failure or low albumin.

faq.q: What is the most common anterior mediastinal mass in young adults?
faq.a: Thymoma, followed closely by lymphoma and germ‑cell tumors.
